challenges.name: average-vs-p99-quiz
challenges.title: What the average hides
challenges.description: Read a latency distribution the way an on-call engineer must: who is having a bad time, and which number shows it?

questions.question: In 5 minutes the checkout endpoint served 10,000 requests: 9,850 took about 50 ms, and 150 took about 3,000 ms (waiting on a hot database row). The mobile app gives up after 2.5 s. The dashboard shows the average. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: The average is (9,850 x 50 + 150 x 3,000) / 10,000 = about 94 ms, which looks healthy and is far below the timeout. But the slowest 1.5% of requests - 150 real customers - took 3 s and saw an error. With the nearest-rank definition, p99 is the value at rank 9,900, which falls inside the slow group, so p99 = 3,000 ms while p50 = 50 ms. Averages blend two very different populations into a number that describes neither; percentiles describe how many users experienced at least that latency.

options.text: The average is about 94 ms, far below 2.5 s, so no customer is affected.
The average is about 94 ms, but p99 is 3,000 ms: 1.5% of checkouts exceed the client timeout, and only the tail percentiles show it.
The average is about 1,525 ms, halfway between the fast and the slow requests.
p50 is 3,000 ms, because the slow requests dominate the total time.

questions.question: Which statements about latency metrics and event loop delay are true? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Percentiles cannot be averaged: the mean of ten per-instance p99s is not the p99 of the combined traffic (one hot instance gets diluted). Export histograms - bucket counts add up across instances - and compute the quantile on the summed buckets, for example histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))). Event loop delay measures how late callbacks run: when it rises while traffic is flat, requests are queueing inside the process before any handler code starts. It is not only a CPU-heavy-service problem - GC pauses, large JSON.parse/stringify, synchronous logging or crypto on the main thread all show up there.

options.text: To get the fleet-wide p99, average the p99 reported by each of the 10 instances.
If event loop delay p99 rises while the request rate is flat, requests are waiting inside the process before their handlers run.
For a fleet-wide p99, export latency histograms and aggregate the bucket counts across instances before computing the quantile.
Event loop delay only matters for CPU-heavy services; an I/O-bound API always reports close to 0 ms.

challenges.name: nearest-rank-percentile
challenges.title: Compute p50, p95 and p99 with nearest rank
challenges.description: The checkout dashboard only shows the average latency. Implement percentile(values, p) with the nearest-rank definition from the starter's JSDoc: numeric sort of a copy, rank = ceil(p/100 * n) (at least 1), return the sample at that rank, null for no samples.

tests.name: p50, p90, p95 and p100 of ten checkout latencies
100 samples: the tail that the average hides
Small samples round the rank up; p0 is the minimum
No samples: every percentile is null

challenges.name: load-shedder
challenges.title: Fail fast with a load shedder
challenges.description: Write createLoadShedder({ maxInFlight, maxLagMs }, getLag). admit() rejects a request with reason "lag" when the event loop lag is above maxLagMs, otherwise with "in_flight" when maxInFlight requests are already running, and otherwise accepts it with a release() that frees its slot exactly once. The harness replays a traffic scenario and checks every decision.

tests.name: Accepts up to maxInFlight, then sheds until a slot is free
High event loop lag sheds even an idle instance
Lag is checked before the in-flight limit
Rejected requests never take a slot
Releasing the same request twice frees only one slot
